description: Dolby Laboratories, Inc. engages in the design and manufacture of audio, imaging, accessibility, and other hardware and software solutions for television, broadcast, and live entertainment industries
description_full: Dolby Laboratories, Inc. engages in the design and manufacture of audio, imaging, accessibility, and other hardware and software solutions for television, broadcast, and live entertainment industries in the United States and internationally. The company develops and licenses its audio technologies, such as AAC, HE-AAC, and extended HE-AAC, a digital audio codec solution; AVC, a digital video codec used in STBs, mobile devices, cameras, and broadcast television services and other products; and Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision include encoding technologies that artists use to create more compelling and immersive audio and video experiences. It also provides DD+, an advanced surround sound audio codec technology; Dolby AC-4, an audio codec that uses cutting edge compression; and HEVC, a digital video codec that compresses video. In addition, the company offers Dolby Cinemas, a premium large format cinemas that deliver a Dolby branded premium cinema offering with Dolby Vision, Dolby Atmos, and a Dolby theater design; Dolby.io, a SaaS product of immersive, interactive, and social experiences with real-time engagement for live events, especially sports; and digital cinema servers, cinema processors, amplifiers, loudspeakers, and audio and imaging hardware and software products for the cinema, television, broadcast, communication, and entertainment industries. Further, it provides various services to support theatrical and television production for cinema exhibition, broadcast, and home entertainment. It serves film studios, content creators, post-production facilities, and broadcasters. Dolby Laboratories, Inc. was founded in 1965 and is headquartered in San Francisco, California.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 2K people. Revenue per employee of $658K ranks in the top quartile among Industrials peers. Each employee generates $213K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $63K per employee reflects an ownership culture. Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Dolby Laboratories is a mid-cap industrials business with a $6.1B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 13% against a 9% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 89% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $436M in free cash flow — roughly 32 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.85× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 20% operating margin runs 11pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.78x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-7.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 8% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 7% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 7% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 30% and a beta of 0.79, it is more defensive than the market.
About $45.7M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 36% in the 2020 crash, 33% in the 2022 bear market and 53% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $41.78 (margin of safety -55%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 23%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $35.21 to $50.94 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/FCF 13.9 vs 22.3 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-2%).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 3 covering analysts target $79.00 on average, 22% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 8.7%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.53).
It runs a 89% gross margin and converts 32% of revenue into free cash flow, or 23% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.85x.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 19.4% of revenue on R&D and 9.5% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $702.6M (12% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 8.3, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.5% over 3 years, 3.0% over 5 years and 3.3% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 55% of profits supports about 6.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 5% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 8%.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (2.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.9%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (13 sales, net $3.2M sold).
It returns 4.1% a year to shareholders (2.1% in buybacks and 2.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years, raising it 7.4% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 13.5% of the float, 7.0 days to cover.
people: With about 2,051 employees, each generates about $658K of revenue, 1.8x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 2.6% a year.
That works out to $213K of free cash flow per employee.
Compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
